chunks: There is hardly a hue from which it has not taken a bit
and improved it further by regular polish, lustre, silken brightness and brilliance
It is therefore like scattered blossoms which have not been seasoned by the rains of spring or the sun of the summer
It also sheds its plumage and puts off its dress. They all fall away and grow again
They fall away from the feather stems like the falling of leaves from twigs
and then they begin to join together and grow till they return to the state that existed before their falling away
The new hues do not change from the previous ones, nor does any colour occur in other than its own place
If you carefully look at one hair from the hairs of its feather stems it would look like red rose, then emerald green and then golden yellow
ai.seo_question: How does Nahj al-Balagha describe the beauty and biological processes of bird plumage?
ai.summary: Imam Ali employs this vivid natural imagery to illustrate the concept of *tawhid* (divine unity) through the diversity of creation, a central theme in Shia theological discourse on the signs of God in the universe. The comparison to artificial dyes (*sibgh*) underscores the perfection of natural design, contrasting human-made embellishment with the intrinsic, self-sustaining beauty of God's creation. This passage serves as a contemplative tool (*tadabbur*) for believers to recognize the Creator's power through the meticulous order observed in even the smallest details of avian life.
